questions.question: Which three ConvNet best practices does chapter 9 promise to cover?
questions.answer: Residual connections, batch normalization, and depthwise separable convolutions.
questions.explanation: Listed in the second bullet of 'This chapter covers'.

questions.question: According to the page, what does a model's architecture define?
options: The learning rate schedule
The hypothesis space: the space of functions gradient descent can search over
The size of the training dataset
The loss function
questions.answer: The hypothesis space: the space of functions gradient descent can search over
questions.explanation: The page says architecture choices define the hypothesis space, parameterized by the weights. Learning rate, dataset size and loss are separate training choices.

questions.question: In what sense is choosing an architecture 'like feature engineering'?
questions.answer: Both encode prior knowledge about the problem and its solution; e.g. using convolutions encodes the assumption that relevant image patterns are translation-invariant.
questions.explanation: The page draws this parallel directly.

questions.question: What does training change, and what does the architecture fix?
questions.answer: Training changes the weights; the architecture fixes which functions are representable at all (the hypothesis space).
questions.explanation: The hypothesis space is 'parameterized by the model's weights', so gradient descent moves within it but cannot leave it.

questions.question: Before reading chapter 9, can you say which of its building blocks you already saw (perhaps without explanation) in chapter 8's Xception model?
questions.answer: Xception uses depthwise separable convolutions, batch normalization (the BatchNormalization layers you were told not to unfreeze, p.289) and residual connections.
questions.explanation: p.294 notes Xception is built from repeated SeparableConv blocks; p.289 mentioned its BatchNormalization layers.

questions.question: According to the page, what makes a model architecture good?
options: It has as many parameters as possible.
It reduces the size of the search space or makes it easier to converge to a good point.
It removes the need for gradient descent.
It uses only dense layers.
questions.answer: It reduces the size of the search space or makes it easier to converge to a good point.
questions.explanation: That is the book's definition (in italics on the page). More parameters enlarge the space; architecture helps gradient descent rather than replacing it; and dense-only models are not singled out as good.

questions.question: What are the three ingredients of the MHR formula, and what other word does the book give for 'reuse'?
questions.answer: Modularity, hierarchy, reuse; reuse is another word for abstraction.
questions.explanation: Defined in the first paragraph of section 9.1.

questions.question: Why do the authors say that 'no amount of training data will save' a model with inappropriate architecture choices?
questions.answer: Because the architecture defines which functions the model can represent and how easily gradient descent can find good ones; if the right function isn't reachable or the landscape is too hard to search, more data doesn't change that.
questions.explanation: Follows from the hypothesis-space framing on p.292 and the search-space argument on this page.

questions.question: Give one example of reuse in a ConvNet and explain how it reduces the search space.
questions.answer: Convolution kernels are shared across all spatial positions (and blocks are repeated), so the number of parameters doesn't grow with image size and the model is restricted to translation-invariant pattern detectors.
questions.explanation: p.294 states that convolutions are all about reusing the same information in different spatial locations; the parameter-count reasoning is an AI elaboration.

questions.question: Which three ConvNet best practices does the page announce for the following sections?
options: Dropout, weight decay, early stopping
Residual connections, batch normalization, separable convolution
Data augmentation, feature extraction, fine-tuning
Max pooling, strides, padding
questions.answer: Residual connections, batch normalization, separable convolution
questions.explanation: Named explicitly on the page. Dropout/weight decay are regularization techniques, augmentation/feature extraction/fine-tuning are chapter 8's strategies, and pooling/strides/padding were covered in section 8.1.

questions.question: For a 180×180×3 input, compare the parameter count of a Dense layer with 32 units (on the flattened input) with that of a Conv2D layer with 32 filters of size 3×3.
questions.answer: Dense: 180·180·3·32 + 32 = 3,110,432. Conv2D: 3·3·3·32 + 32 = 896. About 3,500 times fewer parameters for the conv layer.
questions.explanation: Weights = inputs × outputs plus one bias per output; the conv kernel connects only a 3×3×3 window and is shared across positions. An illustration (not from the book) of how architecture shrinks the search space.

questions.question: Think of a codebase you know. Can you point to one module, one level of hierarchy and one instance of reuse, and then name their counterparts in a ConvNet?
questions.answer: Open-ended; e.g. a utility function (module, reused in many files), packages (hierarchy) vs layers (modules), stacked blocks (hierarchy), shared kernels and repeated blocks (reuse).
questions.explanation: The page draws the parallel between software architecture and deep learning architecture.

questions.question: According to the page, which deep learning ingredient is the example of 'reuse'?
options: Stacking layers
Convolutions applying the same information at different spatial locations
Using more filters in deeper layers
Training with gradient descent
questions.answer: Convolutions applying the same information at different spatial locations
questions.explanation: The book says convolutions 'are all about reusing the same information in different spatial locations'. Stacking layers is the hierarchy, more filters describes the pyramid pattern, and gradient descent is the optimization technique being structured.

questions.question: What are blocks (modules) in ConvNet architecture, and what block does Xception repeat?
questions.answer: Repeated groups of layers treated as units; Xception repeats SeparableConv - SeparableConv - MaxPooling blocks.
questions.explanation: The page states that popular ConvNets are structured into repeated groups of layers called blocks or modules, with Xception's SeparableConv - SeparableConv - MaxPooling as the example (Figure 9.2).

questions.question: Describe the pyramid-like structure of ConvNets and explain why it makes sense for the filter count to grow as feature maps shrink.
questions.answer: Spatial size decreases with depth while the number of filters increases. Deeper layers cover larger regions and must represent many more kinds of complex patterns, so they need more channels; the extra channels also compensate for lost spatial resolution and keep compute per stage balanced.
questions.explanation: The book states the pattern (32, 64, 128 filters with shrinking maps). The reasons about pattern richness and balanced compute are explanatory additions beyond the page.

questions.question: In a stage with 32 x 32 feature maps and 64 channels, a 2 x 2 max pooling is applied and the next convolution uses 128 filters (same padding). How many activation values does the new feature map hold compared with the old one?
questions.explanation: Halving height and width divides positions by 4, doubling channels multiplies by 2: net factor 1/2. This illustrates how the pyramid pattern shrinks tensors gently.

questions.question: What does the page call 'the simplest kind of hierarchy' in a deep learning model?
options: A residual connection
A stack of layers
A block of separable convolutions
A feature pyramid
questions.answer: A stack of layers
questions.explanation: The text says layers are organized into a deep hierarchy, 'often just a stack, the simplest kind of hierarchy'. Residual connections come later (p.296); blocks and pyramids are richer structures.

questions.question: Which filter progression from the first ConvNet of chapter 8 does the page recall?
questions.explanation: The page: 'Recall, for example, the progression in the number of convolution filters we used in the first ConvNet we built in the previous chapter: 32, 64, 128.'

questions.question: Pick a familiar complex system (a codebase, a car, a city). Can you name its modules, its hierarchy and its reused parts, and then do the same for a ConvNet you have built?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Mapping MHR onto both a non-ML system and a real model checks that you can use the principle, which is how the book intends it (pp.293-294).

questions.question: What are the input and output shapes of the Xception entry flow in Figure 9.2?
questions.explanation: The caption states the shapes. 180 x 180 to 7 x 7 x 512 is the chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model (p.269); the other options are not from the page.

questions.question: Which three filter counts do the repeated blocks of Figure 9.2 use, and what operation ends each block on the main path?
questions.answer: 128, 256 and 728; each block ends with MaxPooling 3x3, stride 2x2 (before the '+' merge).
questions.explanation: Read directly from the figure labels.

questions.question: Why does the book say deeper hierarchies are 'intrinsically good', and what stops us from making them arbitrarily deep?
questions.answer: Depth encourages feature reuse and therefore abstraction, so deep stacks of narrow layers usually outperform shallow stacks of large layers. The limit is the vanishing-gradient problem: error information fails to propagate through very long chains of layers.
questions.explanation: Both parts are stated in the body paragraph; the remedy, residual connections, is introduced next.

questions.question: The first layer is a 3x3 convolution with stride 2 and no padding on a 299 x 299 input. Show that its output is 149 x 149.
questions.explanation: Output size for valid padding is floor((n - k)/s) + 1. This matches the 149 x 149 x 32 label in Figure 9.2.

questions.question: In Figure 9.2, what is the purpose of the 'Conv 1x1, stride=2x2' boxes on the left?
options: They add extra nonlinearity to the main path
They project the block input to the block output's shape so it can be added at '+'
They replace max pooling in the second block
They normalize activations
questions.answer: They project the block input to the block output's shape so it can be added at '+'
questions.explanation: They lie on a separate branch that joins at the addition node: a residual connection whose stride and 1x1 filters match the downsampled spatial size and the new channel count. They add no nonlinearity, do not replace pooling (each block still has pooling) and do not normalize.

questions.question: What does the sidebar mean by saying deep learning architectures are 'more evolved than designed'?
questions.answer: They were developed by repeatedly trying things and keeping what seemed to work, rather than being derived from principles, so like biological systems they may contain components that are not actually needed.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of the sidebar; p.296 completes the thought and recommends ablation studies.

questions.question: Without looking, sketch one Xception entry-flow block with both branches and label the shapes before and after for the 256-filter block.
questions.answer: Input 74 x 74 x 128; main path ReLU, SeparableConv 256, ReLU, SeparableConv 256, MaxPool 3x3/2; shortcut Conv 1x1 stride 2 with 256 filters; sum gives 37 x 37 x 256.
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce this, you understand both the block reuse and the residual merge in Figure 9.2.

questions.question: You found that a model with components X + Y + Z works well. Which configurations does the book suggest also trying?
questions.answer: X, Y, Z, X + Y, X + Z and Y + Z.
questions.explanation: That is the ablation recipe given in the sidebar: every simpler combination, to identify where performance comes from.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, what is the most straightforward way to generate reliable knowledge?
options: Publishing in peer-reviewed venues
Understanding causality in your system
Adding mathematical formalism
Training larger models
questions.answer: Understanding causality in your system
questions.explanation: The book states 'understanding causality in your system is the most straightforward way to generate reliable knowledge.' It criticizes publication incentives and decorative math, and does not mention model size here.

questions.question: Explain the game-of-telephone analogy for backpropagation in y = f4(f3(f2(f1(x)))). Which function's update suffers most, and why?
questions.answer: Each function is a player relaying a message; the message is the error information flowing back from the loss. Each function adds noise, so after several relays the information is corrupted. f1 suffers most, because its error information has to pass through f4, f3 and f2.
questions.explanation: Directly from the last paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Suppose each layer multiplies the backpropagated signal by 0.8 on average. Roughly how strong is the signal reaching the first layer of a 10-layer chain, relative to the output?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, the gradient is a product of per-layer factors (an AI-added formalization of the book's description). Ten factors of 0.8 give about 0.107; at 30 layers it would be about 0.0012.

questions.question: What does the book say happens when the function chain is too deep?
options: The model overfits the training data
Noise overwhelms gradient information and the model won't train at all
The learning rate must be increased
The model becomes translation-invariant
questions.answer: Noise overwhelms gradient information and the model won't train at all
questions.explanation: That is the definition of the vanishing-gradient problem on the page. Overfitting requires that the model fits the data; learning rate and translation invariance are not discussed here.

questions.question: What kind of test does 'replace some trained features with random ones' represent, and what would it show?
questions.answer: An ablation-style test; if performance is unchanged, the training of those features did not contribute to the result.
questions.explanation: The sidebar uses it as an example of how complex setups often contain parts that don't matter.

questions.question: Think of a model you trained that has several 'tricks' (augmentation, dropout, a learning-rate schedule, etc.). Could you name which one actually contributes, and how would you design an ablation to find out?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Applying the X + Y + Z recipe to your own work is the sidebar's main advice.

questions.question: What does a residual connection do?
options: Multiplies a block's output by its input
Adds a block's input back to its output
Concatenates the outputs of two parallel blocks
Normalizes the block's output
questions.answer: Adds a block's input back to its output
questions.explanation: The book: 'just add the input of a layer or block of layers back to its output.' Multiplication and concatenation are different merges; normalization is batch normalization (p.300).

questions.question: Which model family introduced residual connections, when and by whom?
questions.answer: ResNet, 2015, He et al. at Microsoft.
questions.explanation: Stated in the text and footnote 1 (Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, CVPR 2015).

questions.question: Why can the block in Listing 9.1 be 'destructive or noisy' without harming the model?
questions.answer: Because the original input is added back to its output, the final output always contains full information about the input, and gradients have a direct path back through the addition regardless of what the block does.
questions.explanation: This is the meaning of the callouts in Listing 9.1 and the 'information shortcut' description.

questions.question: A block maps a (None, 30, 30, 32) tensor to (None, 30, 30, 64). How many parameters does the 1x1 Conv2D projection of the residual need?
questions.explanation: A 1x1 conv has kernel 1*1*C_in*C_out weights plus C_out biases.

questions.question: A target block ends with MaxPooling2D(2). What should the residual projection use?
options: A 3x3 Conv2D with ReLU
A 1x1 Conv2D with strides=2 and no activation
padding='valid' to shrink the residual
A Dense layer
questions.answer: A 1x1 Conv2D with strides=2 and no activation
questions.explanation: The book: use a 1 x 1 Conv2D with no activation and strides in the projection to match downsampling caused by max pooling. A 3x3 ReLU conv would be a nonlinear, destructive projection; valid padding would not give the right size; a Dense layer would act on the wrong axis.

questions.question: Why does the book recommend padding='same' in the convolution layers of the target block?
questions.answer: To avoid spatial downsampling due to padding, so the block output keeps the residual's height and width (leaving only pooling to be matched by strides).
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph on shape matching.

questions.question: Can you rewrite Listing 9.1 as runnable Keras code for a block of two Conv2D(64, 3) layers on a (32, 32, 64) input, and say what changes if the block outputs 128 channels?
questions.answer: Use padding='same' convolutions and layers.add; for 128 channels add residual = layers.Conv2D(128, 1)(residual) before the add.
questions.explanation: Checks that you can apply both the basic pattern and the projection rule.

questions.question: In Listing 9.2, why is residual = layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual) needed?
questions.answer: The residual has 32 channels but the block output has 64; the 1x1 conv projects the residual to 64 channels so they can be added.
questions.explanation: From the callout: 'The residual only had 32 filters, so we use a 1 x 1 Conv2D to project it to the correct shape.'

questions.question: Why does Listing 9.3 use strides=2 in the residual projection?
options: To add nonlinearity
To match the downsampling created by the max pooling layer
To reduce the number of parameters
To avoid padding
questions.answer: To match the downsampling created by the max pooling layer
questions.explanation: The callout says so explicitly. The projection has no activation, its parameter count does not depend on strides, and padding is handled by padding='same' in the block.

questions.question: Give the output shapes of the block path and the residual path in Listing 9.3 just before layers.add.
questions.answer: Both are (None, 15, 15, 64).
questions.explanation: Input 32x32x3 -> Conv2D(32,3) valid: 30x30x32 (residual). Block: Conv2D(64, same) 30x30x64 -> MaxPool(2, same) 15x15x64. Residual: Conv2D(64,1,strides=2) -> 15x15x64.

questions.question: Why do both the Conv2D and the MaxPooling2D layers in Listing 9.3 use padding='same'?
questions.answer: To avoid downsampling due to padding, so the only change in spatial size is the intentional factor of 2 from pooling, which the strided projection can match exactly.
questions.explanation: Stated in the callout above Listing 9.3; without same padding the sizes would not line up.

questions.question: What does the pooling argument of residual_block control?
options: Whether the block uses ReLU
Whether the block ends with 2x2 max pooling and a strided residual projection
Whether a residual connection is used at all
The number of filters
questions.answer: Whether the block ends with 2x2 max pooling and a strided residual projection
questions.explanation: Inside `if pooling:` the code adds MaxPooling2D(2, padding='same') and Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2) on the residual. ReLU is always used, the residual is always added, and filters is a separate argument.

questions.question: What does Rescaling(1.0 / 255) do at the start of the example model?
questions.answer: It scales pixel values from the 0-255 range to 0-1 before the convolutions.
questions.explanation: Same preprocessing as the chapter 8 ConvNets.

questions.question: Without running it, predict what error would occur if you deleted the residual projection line from Listing 9.3, and why.
questions.answer: layers.add would raise a shape mismatch: (None, 15, 15, 64) vs (None, 30, 30, 32).
questions.explanation: Tests that you can do shape bookkeeping for residual connections.

questions.question: When pooling=False, under what condition does residual_block project the residual?
questions.answer: Only when filters != residual.shape[-1], i.e. when the number of channels changes.
questions.explanation: From the elif branch and its callout.

questions.question: Why does the third residual block use pooling=False?
options: Because 128 filters cannot be pooled
Because global average pooling is applied right after it
Because the residual projection would fail
To increase the number of parameters
questions.answer: Because global average pooling is applied right after it
questions.explanation: The callout says the last block doesn't need max pooling since global average pooling follows. Pooling works with any filter count, the projection would work with strides, and parameters are not the reason.

questions.question: Verify the 128 parameters of conv2d_8 and explain why its input has 3 channels.
questions.answer: 1*1*3*32 + 32 = 128. It projects the residual of the first block, which is the rescaled input image with 3 channels.
questions.explanation: The 'Connected to' column shows rescaling[0][0] as its input.

questions.question: Compute the parameter count of conv2d_10 and check it against the summary.
questions.answer: 3*3*64*64 + 64 = 36,928, matching the table.
questions.explanation: Kernel 3x3, 64 input channels (from conv2d_9), 64 filters, plus biases.

questions.question: How can you tell from the summary that the model has residual connections, even though there is no explicit 'residual' label?
questions.answer: Some Conv2D layers (e.g. conv2d_8) are connected to an earlier tensor (rescaling) rather than the previous row, and Add layers (add_2) take two inputs, the main path and that projection.
questions.explanation: The Connected to column encodes the graph; branches and merges indicate shortcuts.

questions.question: What is the output shape after max_pooling2d_2?
questions.explanation: Read from the table: block 2's convolutions are 16 x 16 x 64 and 2x2 pooling halves height and width. (None, 8, 8, 128) is block 3's output; the others are earlier layers.

questions.question: Could you modify the model to have six residual blocks (two per width) and predict which blocks would use identity shortcuts?
questions.answer: The second block at each width (same filters, no pooling) would use the identity shortcut; the others would project.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of the three shortcut cases in residual_block.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count of conv2d_13 (Conv2D, 128 filters, 3x3 kernel, input from conv2d_12 with 128 channels).
questions.explanation: A Conv2D has k_h*k_w*C_in*C_out kernel weights plus one bias per filter. This matches the printed 147,584.

questions.question: Why does conv2d_14 have only 8,320 parameters while conv2d_12, which also maps 64 to 128 channels, has 73,856?
options: conv2d_14 is a 1x1 convolution on the residual path, conv2d_12 a 3x3 main-path convolution
conv2d_14 has no bias
conv2d_14 uses strides=2
conv2d_14 shares its weights with conv2d_12
questions.answer: conv2d_14 is a 1x1 convolution on the residual path, conv2d_12 a 3x3 main-path convolution
questions.explanation: 1*1*64*128+128 = 8,320 vs 3*3*64*128+128 = 73,856: the factor of 9 comes from kernel area. Bias is present in both, stride does not change parameter count, and Keras layers do not share weights here.

questions.question: In the book's words, what is normalization in machine learning?
questions.answer: A broad category of methods that seek to make different samples seen by a model more similar to each other, helping it learn and generalize to new data.
questions.explanation: This is the definition at the start of section 9.3; mean/std standardization is the most common instance.

questions.question: The input to a Dense layer has zero mean and unit variance. Give two reasons its output after a ReLU will generally not.
questions.answer: The bias b and the weights W shift and rescale the data (mean b, covariance WW^T), and ReLU discards negative values so the mean becomes positive. Both also change as weights are updated during training.
questions.explanation: This expands the authors' statement that there is no a priori reason for outputs to stay normalized, which motivates normalizing intermediate activations.

questions.question: What assumption do the authors say mean/std normalization makes about the data?
options: That it follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution
That it lies in the 0-1 range
That it is uniformly distributed
That all features are independent
questions.answer: That it follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution
questions.explanation: The page says it 'makes the assumption that the data follows a normal (or Gaussian) distribution' and centers and scales it to unit variance. The 0-1 range belongs to rescaling (p.203); uniformity and independence are not mentioned.

questions.question: Normalize the values [1, 3, 5, 7] with the page's formula (np.std divides by N).
questions.explanation: Deviations are -3, -1, 1, 3; squared mean (9+1+1+9)/4 = 5; dividing each deviation by sqrt(5) gives the z-scores.

questions.question: Can you point to every residual merge in the model summary on pp.299-300 and say which layer is the main path and which is the shortcut?
questions.answer: add_2: max_pooling2d_1 (main) + conv2d_8 (shortcut); add_3: max_pooling2d_2 (main) + conv2d_11 (shortcut); add_4: conv2d_13 (main) + conv2d_14 (shortcut).
questions.explanation: Shortcut layers are the 1x1 Conv2D layers whose input is the previous block's output (rescaling, add_2, add_3).

questions.question: Which statistics does a BatchNormalization layer use at inference time?
options: Exponential moving averages of the batchwise mean and variance seen during training
The mean and variance of the current inference batch
The mean and variance of the full training set computed once before training
Fixed values of 0 and 1
questions.answer: Exponential moving averages of the batchwise mean and variance seen during training
questions.explanation: The page says inference uses an exponential moving average of batchwise statistics because a big enough representative batch may not be available. Current-batch statistics are the training behavior; a one-off full-dataset pass and fixed 0/1 are not what the layer does.

questions.question: Why can a Conv2D layer followed by BatchNormalization be created with use_bias=False?
questions.answer: Because the normalization step centers the layer's output on zero, which cancels any bias, so the bias vector is not needed.
questions.explanation: Subtracting the per-channel batch mean removes any constant per-channel offset, so the bias would have no effect (and zero gradient). The book notes this makes the layer slightly leaner.

questions.question: What is the authors' position on the claim that batch normalization works by 'reducing internal covariate shift', and what broader lesson do they draw?
questions.answer: They say no one really knows why batch normalization helps; there are hypotheses but no certainties. Broader lesson: deep learning is a set of empirically derived engineering best practices woven together by unreliable narratives, and the book often knows the how but not the why.
questions.explanation: This is the second printed paragraph of the page. It warns the reader not to take mechanistic stories at face value.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the main practical effect of batch normalization?
options: It helps with gradient propagation and thus allows deeper networks
It reduces the number of parameters
It replaces the need for data augmentation
It makes models invariant to rotations
questions.answer: It helps with gradient propagation and thus allows deeper networks
questions.explanation: The page says this explicitly, comparing it to residual connections. It actually adds a few parameters (only the bias can be dropped); augmentation and rotation invariance are unrelated.

questions.question: A channel's training batch contains the values [2, 4, 6, 8]. Compute the batch-normalized values (ignore epsilon, gamma=1, beta=0). Then, with momentum 0.99 and a running mean of 0, what is the updated running mean?
questions.explanation: Normalization uses the batch's own mean and variance; the running average moves only 1% of the way toward the new batch mean per step, which is why it reflects the long-run statistics.

questions.question: Why would using the current batch's statistics at inference be a problem when predicting one image at a time?
questions.answer: A single sample (or a small batch) gives unreliable statistics, and predictions would depend on which other samples share the batch; moving averages make the transformation fixed and deterministic.
questions.explanation: The book's phrasing is that a big enough batch of representative data may not be available at inference.

questions.question: Can you write the three-line Keras snippet from the page from memory, and say where the activation should go according to the authors?
questions.answer: x = ...; x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False)(x); x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x). The activation is recommended after the batch normalization layer (debated), as shown on p.302.
questions.explanation: The Conv2D has no activation and no bias; the activation is applied after normalization.

questions.question: Which code reflects the authors' recommended ordering?
options: Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False) -> BatchNormalization() -> Activation("relu")
Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu") -> BatchNormalization()
BatchNormalization() -> Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")
Conv2D(32, 3) -> Activation("relu") -> BatchNormalization() -> Activation("relu")
questions.answer: Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False) -> BatchNormalization() -> Activation("relu")
questions.explanation: The second snippet on the page puts the activation after BN and drops the bias. The second option is the 'instead of' case; the others are not discussed and the last applies ReLU twice.

questions.question: What intuitive reason do the authors give for normalizing before the ReLU?
questions.answer: BN centers inputs on zero, and ReLU uses zero as the pivot for keeping or dropping values, so normalizing first maximizes the utilization of the ReLU.
questions.explanation: They also note the ordering is not critical.

questions.question: Why should BatchNormalization layers be kept frozen when fine-tuning, even though the learning rate is small?
questions.answer: Because otherwise they keep updating their internal mean and variance from the new data, and these statistic updates are not limited by the learning rate; the resulting shifts interfere with the very small updates applied to the surrounding Conv2D layers.
questions.explanation: The NOTE on the page; it is the explanation promised on p.289.

questions.question: What does a depthwise separable convolution do?
options: A spatial convolution on each input channel independently, then a 1x1 pointwise convolution to mix channels
A 1x1 convolution followed by max pooling
Two regular 3x3 convolutions in sequence
A convolution that ignores spatial structure entirely
questions.answer: A spatial convolution on each input channel independently, then a 1x1 pointwise convolution to mix channels
questions.explanation: This is the page's definition (figure 9.4 on p.303). It does not involve pooling, is not two full convolutions, and the depthwise stage does capture spatial structure.

questions.question: Compute the number of weights (no biases) of a regular 3x3 Conv2D and of a 3x3 SeparableConv2D, both mapping 32 to 64 channels.
questions.explanation: Depthwise stage: one 3x3 filter per input channel; pointwise stage: a 32x64 channel-mixing matrix.

questions.question: What assumption about intermediate activations does depthwise separable convolution rely on, and what analogous assumption does regular convolution make?
questions.answer: Separable: spatial locations are highly correlated but different channels are highly independent. Regular convolution: patterns in images are not tied to specific locations.
questions.explanation: Both are priors built into the architecture; the page draws the parallel explicitly.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why use_bias=False is fine in the recommended snippet but not obviously so in the 'instead of' snippet?
questions.answer: In the recommended snippet, BN directly follows the convolution and subtracts the mean, cancelling any bias. In the other snippet, a ReLU sits between the bias and BN, so the bias changes which values ReLU keeps and is not cancelled.
questions.explanation: Connects the NOTE on p.301 with the ordering on this page.

questions.question: Reproduce the sidebar's two parameter counts for a 3x3 convolution with 64 input and 64 output channels.
questions.explanation: The regular kernel couples spatial and channel dimensions; the separable version pays for them separately.

questions.question: For a 5x5 window with 128 input and 128 output channels, compute both parameter counts and their ratio (no biases).
questions.explanation: Confirms the sidebar's claim that savings grow with window size and filter count; the ratio formula is 25*128/(25+128).

questions.question: In figure 9.4, which operation mixes information across channels?
options: The 1x1 conv (pointwise conv)
The 3x3 convs
Split channels
Concatenate
questions.answer: The 1x1 conv (pointwise conv)
questions.explanation: The 3x3 convs are independent per channel (the callout says so), splitting and concatenating only rearrange data. Only the pointwise conv combines channels.

questions.question: Complete the authors' principle: 'A model with stronger priors about the structure of the information it will have to process is a better model—...'
questions.answer: '...as long as the priors are accurate.'
questions.explanation: An inaccurate prior would constrain the model in the wrong way.

questions.question: Why are the advantages of separable convolutions 'especially important when you're training small models from scratch on limited data'?
questions.answer: With limited data, overfitting and data efficiency are the main problems. Fewer parameters reduce overfitting, and an accurate prior lets the model learn more from each sample and converge faster.
questions.explanation: Large pretrained or data-rich settings are less constrained by these issues.

questions.question: Which high-performing ConvNet packaged with Keras is based on depthwise separable convolutions?
options: Xception
VGG16
AlexNet
LeNet
questions.answer: Xception
questions.explanation: Named on the page, with the 2017 CVPR paper in footnote 3. VGG16, AlexNet and LeNet use regular convolutions.

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 9.4 from memory and label which part accounts for most of the 4,672 parameters?
questions.answer: Split channels -> per-channel 3x3 convs -> concatenate -> 1x1 pointwise conv. The pointwise conv holds 4,096 of the 4,672 parameters.
questions.explanation: For many channels, the pointwise stage dominates the cost of a separable convolution.

questions.question: Why are depthwise separable convolutions only about as fast as regular convolutions on GPUs?
options: Regular convolutions run as cuDNN kernels optimized down to machine instructions, while separable convolutions have not received comparable optimization
Separable convolutions actually require more FLOPs
GPUs cannot execute 1x1 convolutions
Separable convolutions must run on the CPU
questions.answer: Regular convolutions run as cuDNN kernels optimized down to machine instructions, while separable convolutions have not received comparable optimization
questions.explanation: The sidebar attributes the gap to optimization effort, not arithmetic. Separable convolutions need fewer FLOPs (p.303), GPUs run 1x1 convolutions fine, and they do run on GPUs.

questions.question: Where does the book say you do see a meaningful speedup from separable convolutions?
questions.answer: On CPU, where the underlying implementation is parallelized C++ (and in simple CUDA/C++ implementations generally).
questions.explanation: Without cuDNN-level optimization of the alternative, the FLOP savings translate into speed.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors still recommend separable convolutions when they bring no speedup.
questions.answer: Their lower parameter count reduces the risk of overfitting, and their assumption that channels are uncorrelated leads to faster convergence and more robust representations.
questions.explanation: Both are statistical benefits, independent of runtime.

questions.question: Explain the co-evolution loop the authors describe and one consequence for researchers proposing new algorithms.
questions.answer: GPUs and CUDA enabled early success of backprop-trained ConvNets; NVIDIA then optimized hardware and software for them; the community consolidated behind them. Consequence: a new algorithm (e.g. spiking networks or gradient-free optimization) would first run orders of magnitude slower, making it a tough sell even if it were better.
questions.explanation: The authors conclude that a different path would require a multiyear reengineering of the ecosystem.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the ConvNet principles listed on this page?
options: The number of filters should increase as the spatial size of the feature maps decreases
The number of filters should stay constant throughout the network
Max pooling should be avoided in blocks
Every layer should be a Dense layer
questions.answer: The number of filters should increase as the spatial size of the feature maps decreases
questions.explanation: That is the second bullet. The first bullet explicitly includes max pooling in blocks; constant filters and Dense-only layers contradict the chapter.

questions.question: Can you name two alternative algorithm families the authors say would struggle against the hardware/software ecosystem, and say why?
questions.answer: Gradient-free optimization and spiking neural networks: their first parallel C++/CUDA implementations would be orders of magnitude slower than an optimized ConvNet.
questions.explanation: Speed governs how many experiments are feasible and how convincing results are.

questions.question: Why is the first convolution in the model a regular Conv2D rather than a SeparableConv2D?
options: Red, green and blue channels are highly correlated in natural images, so the channel-independence assumption fails
SeparableConv2D cannot accept 3-channel inputs
A 5x5 window is not supported by SeparableConv2D
Regular convolutions are faster on the first layer
questions.answer: Red, green and blue channels are highly correlated in natural images, so the channel-independence assumption fails
questions.explanation: That is the callout's reasoning. SeparableConv2D accepts any channel count and window size; speed is not the argument given.

questions.question: Why does the residual projection use `strides=2` and `padding="same"`?
questions.answer: Because the main path is downsampled by MaxPooling2D(3, strides=2, padding='same'); the projected residual must have the same spatial size (and `size` channels) to be added.
questions.explanation: Both stride-2 'same' operations give ceil(H/2), e.g. 11 -> 6 in the last block.

questions.question: Starting from a 180x180 input, what is the spatial size after the stem Conv2D (5x5, valid) and after each of the five blocks?
questions.answer: 176 after the stem; then 88, 44, 22, 11, 6.
questions.explanation: Valid 5x5: 180 - 4 = 176. Each block halves with rounding up: ceil(11/2) = 6.

questions.question: Every convolution in the code has use_bias=False. Justify this for the SeparableConv2D layers and for the residual projection.
questions.answer: The first SeparableConv2D of each block is followed directly by BatchNormalization, which subtracts the per-channel mean and cancels any constant bias. The second one and the residual projection feed the add; whatever constant they would contribute is cancelled by the next block's first BatchNormalization on the main path. On the shortcut chain it would only propagate as a constant offset through 1x1 convolutions and adds to global average pooling, where the Dense layer's own bias can absorb it. So the biases would be redundant.
questions.explanation: This applies the NOTE on p.301 (normalization centers the output, so the bias is unnecessary) to the less obvious places in this model. The argument for the shortcut chain is our own reasoning, not the book's.

questions.question: Which statement matches a principle listed on this page?
options: Deep and narrow is better than broad and shallow
Broad and shallow is better than deep and narrow
Batch normalization should always be placed before the input rescaling
Separable convolutions should only be used in the first layer
questions.answer: Deep and narrow is better than broad and shallow
questions.explanation: It is the first bullet on the page. The second option is the reverse; the third and fourth contradict the code (rescaling comes first; separable convolutions are used after the first layer).

questions.question: What does the model use instead of chapter 8's Flatten layer, and what shape does it produce here?
questions.answer: GlobalAveragePooling2D, producing (None, 512).
questions.explanation: Stated in the callout; 512 is the last block's filter count.

questions.question: For each of the six principles (p.304 and this page), can you point to the line(s) of the code that implement it?
questions.answer: Blocks: the for-loop body. Increasing filters: [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]. Deep and narrow: ten 3x3 separable convs in five blocks. Residual: residual = x / Conv2D(size, 1, strides=2) / layers.add. Batch normalization: the BatchNormalization lines before each ReLU. SeparableConv2D: the two SeparableConv2D lines per block.
questions.explanation: Mapping principles to code is the purpose of section 9.5.

questions.question: Compared with the chapter 8 ConvNet, the mini Xception-like model has…
options: more parameters and higher test accuracy
fewer parameters and higher test accuracy
fewer parameters and lower test accuracy
about the same number of parameters and the same accuracy
questions.answer: fewer parameters and higher test accuracy
questions.explanation: 721,857 vs. 1,569,089 trainable parameters, and 90.8% vs. 83.9% test accuracy. The options with 'more parameters' or 'lower accuracy' contradict the page's numbers, and the counts differ by more than 2×.

questions.question: Using the page's test accuracies, by what fraction does the new model reduce the test error rate?
questions.answer: About 43%: error goes from 16.1% to 9.2%, and 9.2/16.1 ≈ 0.57.
questions.explanation: Error rate = 1 − accuracy. 1 − 0.839 = 0.161 and 1 − 0.908 = 0.092. The relative reduction is 1 − 0.092/0.161 ≈ 0.43.

questions.question: What does the line `layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` produce, and why one unit?
questions.answer: A single probability in (0, 1) for the positive class; one unit suffices because dogs vs. cats is a binary task.
questions.explanation: The sigmoid maps the logit to a probability; the other class's probability is 1 minus it. This matches the binary setup of chapter 8.

questions.question: Why can a model with fewer parameters outperform a larger one on the dogs-vs-cats task?
questions.answer: Because its architecture encodes better priors and uses capacity efficiently (separable convolutions, global average pooling, residual connections, batch normalization), so it learns more from limited data and has less spare capacity to overfit.
questions.explanation: The page shows the result; the chapter (pp.293, 303) explains that good architecture shrinks the search space and makes efficient use of the data.

questions.question: According to the authors, how was the configuration of the mini Xception model chosen?
options: By an automated hyperparameter search
By copying the full Xception architecture
From the outlined best practices plus a small amount of intuition about model size
By trial and error on the test set
questions.answer: From the outlined best practices plus a small amount of intuition about model size
questions.explanation: The page says explicitly that tuning was not done (that's chapter 18). It is a smaller model that only resembles Xception, and tuning on the test set would be methodologically wrong.

questions.question: What is the book's current recommendation regarding ViTs versus ConvNets?
questions.answer: ViTs are competing with ConvNets and may replace them in the long term, but for now ConvNets remain the best option in most cases.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of section 9.6; p.307 adds that ViTs shine on massive datasets and large models.

questions.question: Look at figure 9.5. Can you describe where the training and validation curves diverge and what that says about overfitting?
questions.answer: Training loss keeps falling to ~0.1 while validation loss stays noisy around 0.4–0.8 after about 40 epochs, a sign of some overfitting; validation accuracy still rises to the high 0.8s.
questions.explanation: Being able to read such curves is essential for deciding when to stop training or add regularization.

questions.question: Describe the three steps by which a ViT turns an image into something a Transformer can process.
questions.answer: Split the image into a 1D sequence of patches, turn each patch into a flat vector, and process the vector sequence.
questions.explanation: Transformers are sequence-processing architectures, so the image must be represented as a sequence of vectors.

questions.question: Which is one of the two reasons the book gives for ViTs being suboptimal on small datasets?
options: They cannot capture long-range relationships
They lack the spatial prior of ConvNets
They cannot be trained with gradient descent
They require labeled text data
questions.answer: They lack the spatial prior of ConvNets
questions.explanation: The two reasons are the missing spatial prior and the need to be very large. Capturing long-range relationships is a ViT strength, not a weakness; ViTs are trained with gradient descent and do not need text.

questions.question: Why does the spatial prior of ConvNets make them more data efficient?
questions.answer: Their 2D local, weight-shared architecture builds in assumptions about the local structure of visual space, so the model does not have to learn those regularities from data; the hypothesis space is smaller.
questions.explanation: This ties to the chapter's thesis (p.292–293) that architecture encodes prior knowledge and helps gradient descent.

questions.question: For which situation do the authors say ConvNets remain your best bet?
options: Large-scale generative image models
Small-scale image classification
Text classification
Any dataset larger than ImageNet
questions.answer: Small-scale image classification
questions.explanation: The page explicitly recommends ConvNets for small-scale image classification. Large generative image models are where you'll likely meet ViTs; text is the Transformer's original domain; datasets larger than ImageNet favour ViTs.

questions.question: Name the three key computer vision architecture patterns listed in the chapter summary.
questions.answer: Residual connections, batch normalization, and depthwise separable convolutions.
questions.explanation: These are sections 9.2, 9.3 and 9.4, combined in the mini Xception model of section 9.5.

questions.question: What is a 'long-range relationship' in an image, and why might a Transformer capture it more easily than a ConvNet?
questions.answer: A dependency between distant image regions. In a Transformer every patch can interact with every other patch directly, while a ConvNet relates distant regions only after many local layers expand its receptive field.
questions.explanation: The page states the capability; the mechanism (self-attention vs. local convolution) is an explanation beyond the book's text.

questions.question: Without looking, can you restate the chapter's first summary bullet and give an example from chapters 8–9 of an architecture encoding an assumption?
questions.answer: The architecture of a deep learning model encodes key assumptions about the problem. Example: convolution layers encode the assumption that relevant visual patterns are local and translation-invariant; separable convolutions assume channels are largely independent.
questions.explanation: Both examples come from the chapter (p.292 and the p.305 callout).
